title: Japan puts a price on ten-year money and a condition on the exit
summary: On 21 September 2016 the Bank of Japan gave two signals to different parts of the market. Bond dealers received a yield objective for ten-year government debt, near the level already prevailing. Households and firms received a commitment to continued monetary-base expansion even after a first encounter with 2% inflation. A series that records only changes in the overnight policy rate would mark this meeting as a hold. It would miss a change in which market price the Bank intended to defend and what inflation evidence it would accept before ending base expansion (sections 2 and 3).

The Bank left the rate on designated policy-rate balances at −0.1% and set the ten-year Japanese government bond (JGB) yield objective at roughly zero. The previous pace of about ¥80 trillion a year referred to the increase in the stock of JGBs held by the Bank. It remained an approximate guide, while the yield objective would govern purchases. The Bank also removed its guideline for the average remaining maturity of purchases. If investors were willing to hold ten-year debt near the target, achieving it could require fewer purchases. If they sold aggressively, more purchases could be necessary. A change in the purchase pace would consequently have an ambiguous meaning without the yield and market conditions alongside it (pp. 1–2).

Two operating tools made that change credible. The Bank could specify a yield at which it would buy bonds and could supply fixed-rate funds for up to ten years, extending the previous limit of one year. The decision cited ten- and twenty-year fixed-rate purchases as possible responses to a spike. Only the ten-year yield had an explicit target. Equity fund and real-estate fund holdings were to increase by about ¥6 trillion and ¥90 billion a year respectively. Commercial paper and corporate bond holdings had separate outstanding-stock objectives of about ¥2.2 trillion and ¥3.2 trillion. Treating all four as annual purchases would materially misstate the package (p. 2).

Why promise an overshoot? The Bank’s assessment linked weaker inflation expectations to the fall in oil prices, weaker demand after the April 2014 consumption tax increase, and slowing emerging economies accompanied by volatile markets. With households and firms taking cues from recent inflation, those developments could depress expected inflation and raise real borrowing costs even if nominal rates stayed low. The commitment concerned observed year-on-year CPI excluding fresh food. Base expansion would continue until inflation exceeded 2% and stayed above it on a stable basis. Forecast inflation reaching 2% would leave that condition open. The Bank allowed short-run variation in base growth while it pursued the yield objective and did not specify a required number of above-target readings (pp. 3–4 and Attachment 1, sections A–C).

How far should the curve fall? The Bank reported that lower JGB yields had already translated into lower bank lending rates and cheaper bonds and commercial paper. Banks had absorbed part of the decline through narrower lending margins. The next reduction in the sovereign curve could therefore have a different effect on loan prices or credit supply. Short and medium maturities mattered most directly for activity in the majority’s assessment, although firms issuing very long bonds could change that relationship. Excessive flattening could also cause households to question the viability of financial institutions. The decision supported continued easing while making the shape of the curve a policy choice in its own right (Attachment 1, sections D–E).

The 7–2 vote on the operating guideline concealed two distinct objections. Takehiro Sato worried that the two rate settings might leave yields negative out to ten years and impair intermediation. Takahide Kiuchi preferred a positive short rate of 0.1% and opposed setting a long yield partly because it might require faster JGB buying. The new operational tools passed 8–1, with Sato joining the majority. A single vote count would lose the distinction between supporting an instrument and supporting the price at which it would be used (p. 5).

At the meeting, CPI excluding fresh food was slightly negative, inflation expectations had weakened recently and exports and production were broadly flat. The Bank expected weak energy prices to keep measured inflation near zero or slightly below it for a time. Event analysis should preserve this information set. The release reference gives 13:18 Japan time, twenty minutes after the meeting ended. Measuring from the end of deliberations would mix an interval without the published decision into the announcement response. The direction of changes in the yen, yields and bank shares after release requires separate market observations (Attachment 2 and release reference).

questions.question: Did the ten-year target change the shape of the curve at the release?
questions.detail: Compare the last executable two-, five-, ten- and twenty-year JGB quotes before 13:18 Japan time with quotes one, five and thirty minutes later. A localized move at ten years would support a benchmark-specific interpretation. A common move across the curve would call for comparison with swap rates and overseas yields. Record stale quotes and the timing of subsequent press remarks separately.

questions.question: Could purchases slow even while yield control stayed effective?
questions.detail: Join purchase-operation announcements and results by maturity with deviations of the ten-year yield from zero. Distinguish gross purchases, redemptions and the resulting change in outstanding holdings. Falling net additions alongside stable yields would fit a lower quantity needed to maintain the target. Rising yields alongside falling additions would require a different explanation, including shifts in expected policy.

questions.question: Did the overshooting pledge move expected inflation independently of energy prices?
questions.detail: Compare inflation compensation around the release with later household and firm surveys whose fieldwork dates are known. Allow for liquidity in inflation-linked bonds and oil-price changes over the survey window. An intraday change in compensation can reflect risk premia, while a persistent survey shift would provide evidence about beliefs among actual price and wage setters.

questions.question: Where did lower yields cease to pass through to borrowers?
questions.detail: Track bank loan rates, interest margins, lending attitudes and corporate bond issuance by maturity after the decision. Split banks by their reliance on deposit funding and firms by access to capital markets. A cheaper bond issue for a large borrower and a smaller loan margin at a regional lender would capture different distributional effects of the same curve.
